Existing memory systems, however, are primarily designed for general-purpose conversations and do not sufficiently coordinate conversational information with the structured code entities to which it refers. We propose ReConMem, a graph-based dual memory system for repository-oriented conversations. ReConMem organizes distilled conversational memories and conversation-relevant code entities into interconnected semantic and structural memory graphs, while maintaining their cross-graph associations as interactions evolve. For memory recall, ReConMem combines natural-language and code-aligned retrieval through code-draft-based query grounding, expands retrieved information over intra- and inter-graph relations, and compresses retrieved code according to its structural granularity. We evaluate ReConMem on two repository-oriented conversational benchmarks spanning long-horizon context management and realistic project-grounded multi-turn assistance. On LoCoEval, ReConMem improves Pass@1 over the strongest baseline by 7.917 and 7.292 percentage points on single-hop and multi-hop subsets, respectively, with comparable context compression. On CodeAssistBench, it achieves 27.61% Correct and 44.03% Partially Correct, exceeding Full History by 4.10 and 7.09 percentage points, respectively, while improving interaction quality. These results demonstrate that aligning conversational memory with repository structure improves context management for repository-oriented multi-turn interactions.

papers.title: Generalized Frequency-Domain Stability Analysis Formulation for Multi-Terminal HVDC Systems
papers.abstract: The integration of offshore wind farms (OWFs) and the interconnection of different transmission networks are key drivers for multi-terminal DC (MTDC) systems. Bipolar high-voltage direct current (HVDC) employing dedicated metallic return (DMR) are attractive due to their increased availability, which co-exist with monopolar and rigid bipole configurations. While existing works focus on symmetric operation and particular configurations, we present a unified framework for MTDC stability analysis valid for both symmetric and asymmetric conditions. The formulation uses the minimum number of variables without loss of information, and combines the analytical network representation with black-box converter models, thereby enabling sensitivity studies. In addition, a closed-form expression guiding the stability improvement is presented, which requires minimal data exchange between involved parties. The framework is demonstrated on several case studies of increasing complexity, which highlight the importance of considering intra-station converter couplings and possible uncertainty of network parameters.

papers.title: RIVER: Evidence-guided multi-agent retrieval for enzyme--reaction discovery
papers.abstract: Enzyme function annotation and the identification of candidate enzymes for a given reaction are essential steps in connecting genomic information to biochemical reaction networks. However, existing methods rely on sequence or structural similarity or on training with known enzyme--reaction pairs, making it difficult to integrate biochemical evidence across large candidate spaces; they also struggle with retrieval tasks involving enzyme families whose members are highly similar. Here, we introduce RIVER (Reaction--enzyme Inference via Evidence-guided Retrieval), a multi-agent framework for bidirectional enzyme--reaction retrieval that identifies potentially catalyzed reactions for a given enzyme and ranks candidate enzymes for a given reaction. RIVER coordinates large language models, specialized biochemical computational tools, and external knowledge resources to assemble evidence at multiple levels, including reaction chemistry, protein sequences and domains, catalytic mechanisms, and database annotations. Dedicated validation modules further examine evidence gaps and potential conflicts and rerank candidates using traceable evidence records. On public benchmarks, RIVER achieves the highest success rates in both enzyme retrieval and enzyme annotation. In family-specific enzyme retrieval, RIVER outperforms the evaluated baselines on the selected datasets and metrics. In Escherichia coli enzyme retrieval tasks constructed from recent literature, RIVER achieves the best retrieval results with closed-source and open-source model configurations, substantially outperforming closed-source general-purpose and biology-specialized multi-agent systems, including Claude Code, Codex, and Phylo Max. These results suggest that evidence-guided multi-agent retrieval can prioritize biochemically supported enzyme--reaction relationships, providing a basis for subsequent experimental validation.

papers.title: Scaling Laws for SAE Training Data
papers.abstract: Activation storage is often a bottleneck in sparse autoencoder (SAE) training. We study how many unique activations an SAE needs when its total training budget is fixed. Quality improves rapidly as the buffer grows, then reaches a plateau where replaying the buffer is nearly as effective as using fresh activations throughout training. Beyond this point, additional unique activations bring little benefit to reconstruction or interpretability, so the buffer need not grow with the training budget. We describe this tradeoff between diversity and repetition with a scaling law for limited data. We validate it across dictionary sizes and token budgets, early, middle, and late layers of Llama-3.1, Qwen3 model sizes, and BatchTopK, TopK, and JumpReLU SAEs. Sweeps using mathematical text and Python code test the effect of changing the activation source. Evaluation covers explained variance (EV), reconstruction MSE, feature absorption, automated interpretability, and sparse probing. These results give a practical training rule: choose the smallest buffer that reaches the quality plateau and replay it for the remaining budget. In our experiments, this reduces activation storage by $8\text{--}64\times$ with negligible quality loss.

papers.title: Automated Video-to-QA Pipeline: End-to-End Question Generation and Verification Using Large Language Models
papers.abstract: The exponential growth of educational and informational video content on platforms like YouTube presents a challenge for efficient knowledge retrieval and assessment. This paper proposes an end-to-end automated pipeline for extracting structured summaries and generating high-fidelity Question-Answer (QA) pairs from video streams. The framework integrates a cascade of state-of-the-art models: audio extraction is handled via FFmpeg, followed by automatic speech recognition (ASR) using Whisper (A library in Python) to generate accurate transcripts. Due to the token constraints of Large Language Models (LLMs), transcripts are segmented and summarized using Facebook's BART. A key innovation of this work is a Self-Verification and Fine-Tuning Loop. We utilize meta-llama/Llama-3.1-8BInstruct to generate candidate QA pairs from transcript chunks, which are then fed back into the model to rigorously assess their relevance and importance. Only verified, high-quality pairs are retained to construct a synthetic dataset. This dataset is subsequently used to fine-tune the Llama model using Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA), resulting in a specialized model capable of generating domain-aligned assessment questions. This approach demonstrates a scalable method for creating self-improving educational tools without the need for manual data annotation. The proposed model can be downloaded from Kaggle with all the codes from GitHub.

papers.title: Uncovering Systematic Blind Spots in Graph Database Testing through Integration and Process-Level Analysis
papers.abstract: Graph databases are becoming foundational infrastructure for connected data, and a growing body of automated testing techniques has uncovered many bugs across mature graph database systems. Each technique checks a different aspect of correctness and exposes a different class of defect. Combining them is the natural next step, but each technique is judged by the real bugs it finds, not by useless reports or tests that can never fail, and that is what decides whether a developer can afford to fix the problems. To identify the remaining gaps, we integrated test capabilities from 8 testing methods and conducted an empirical study of their behavior, during which we found two blind spots. First, 12 hours of testing produce thousands of bug reports, far more than the number of genuine defects a mature database is likely to contain. Most reports are false positives caused by dialect or pattern-matching differences, and many of the remaining reports are duplicates. Second, analysis of process-level data reveals that many equivalence-based metamorphic test cases lose their ability to detect defects because of the optimization mechanism. Based on these findings, we summarize and realize these guidelines in GraphWeave, an integrated testing platform for graph databases. This includes a multi-agent system that analyzes the flood of bug reports to produce gating rules for issue filtering and adapter rules for dialect adaptation, and a plan-aware triage routes metamorphic pairs by plan, skipping those that share a plan on the same graph state and therefore cannot detect defects. We apply GraphWeave to NeuG, a recently open-sourced industrial graph database that has not been covered by prior graph database testing work. With modest manual effort, GraphWeave uncovers 19 previously unknown bugs, all of which have since been confirmed.

papers.title: Neural Collapse on Imbalanced Datasets and Open-Set Scenario
papers.abstract: Neural collapse (NC) describes the elegant geometric structure that sample features and classifier vectors exhibit when a classification model's loss reaches its minimum. Class imbalance, however, generally distorts standard NC. In this paper, we theoretically reformulate NC on imbalanced datasets and in open-set settings. Our analysis is based on an optimization problem over class-wise averaged losses, rather than the global averaged losses used in prior NC studies. We prove that when class-wise averaged losses attain their minima, standard NC is achieved on balanced or imbalanced datasets, for both cross-entropy (CE) and binary cross-entropy (BCE) losses. We further extend the analysis to an open-set-inspired scenario, where some classes contain no training samples yet are still assigned classifier vectors in the losses. We find that in this scenario, when class-wise averaged losses reach their minima, standard NC still emerges on the known classes with training samples, while the classifier vectors of unknown classes without training samples overlap with each other and become orthogonal to those of the known classes. Finally, we analyze Softmax- and Sigmoid-based contrastive losses re-balanced by inverse sample frequency, proving that at their minima on balanced or imbalanced datasets, sample features of different classes likewise form standard NC.

papers.title: On strongly convex Kähler--Berwald manifolds
papers.abstract: For every real Berwald strongly convex complex Finsler manifold $(M,F,J,\hat\nabla)$, if the Cartan nonlinear connection satisfies the parallelism condition $\hat\nabla J=0$, we construct a good complex vertical connection $D$, prove that $D$ is the complex Rund connection, and $F$ is Kähler-Berwald. The inverse direction also can be seen from the construction and proof. As an application, we prove that on an irreducible Hermitian symmetric space $M=G/H$, $G$-invariant complex Finsler metrics are Kähler--Berwald. Besides, we obtain the characterization of strongly pseudoconvex holomorphically invariant complex Finsler metrics on the classical domains of type-IV.

papers.title: Adjustment-Anchor Dependence in Formulaic Alpha Languages: A Certified Grammar and a Re-Anchoring Audit
papers.abstract: Several public scripts for formulaic alpha mining store prices adjusted to the snapshot's last day, so a past day's stored price changes with every later split or dividend and formulas that do not cancel the adjustment factor depend on future corporate actions. We formalise a change of adjustment anchor as a per-stock group action and give a two-sorted type system that soundly certifies anchor invariance from a formula's syntax, under a declared field-adjustment contract and idealised operator semantics; its second sort admits log-returns, and a linear-time checker plugs into any miner. In a re-anchoring audit on Chinese A-shares, pools that five published methods mined in our benchmark pipeline score a mean information coefficient (IC) 0.005 higher on the stored representation than on a cutoff-anchored one, about 14% of their IC. Certified pools move by 0.001 or less, and pools mined on past-anchored data stay sensitive. On the Chinese development folds, certification shows no detectable predictive cost or gain at the design's resolution, about 0.017 IC across cells on pool ICs of 0.03-0.04. We also trace an erroneous index-membership entry to public Qlib data snapshots and show that re-mining exposes the effect of such data defects, which re-evaluating fixed pools misses.

papers.title: Foresee to Trade: Forecast-Augmented Policy Optimization for Portfolio Management
papers.abstract: Online investment services must translate asset opportunities into investment outcomes for users' accounts, yet the same market opportunity can warrant different account actions. We study how supervision from future asset opportunities can strengthen account-level trading decisions and propose Forecast-Augmented Relative Policy Optimization (FRPO). FRPO separately supervises asset opportunities and account decisions through a jointly learned representation: a Financial State Head (FSH) learns future relative-return targets to provide asset-level opportunity supervision, while Same-Path Group-Relative Optimization compares trading trajectories under the same market path and initial account to provide account-level relative-outcome supervision. An Adaptive Gate coordinates auxiliary supervision using predictive variance and gradient alignment. FSH is used only during training; inference uses the encoder and policy for trading. Across DJIA30, TOPIX Core30, and three investment-style portfolios, ten-seed evaluations show that FRPO achieves the highest mean cumulative and annualized returns among the compared methods in all five settings. These results support strengthening investment agents' trading decisions through joint supervision from asset opportunities and trading outcomes.

papers.title: ConvPE: Convolutional Position Embedding Improves Transformers
papers.abstract: ConvPE (Convolutional Position Embedding) improves both the performance and efficiency of Transformer models in language modeling, long-context extension, and vision. It injects a windowed, content-dependent bias into attention scores through a lightweight causal convolution over a low-dimensional projection of the hidden states. As a lightweight plug-in, ConvPE is compatible with RoPE, attention masks, and KV concatenation. It also supports high-dimensional position embeddings via high-dimensional convolutions. In a reproduction, ConvPE outperforms five 1D baselines and eight 2D baselines. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/wzhagi/convpe.

papers.title: Gravitational Thermodynamicization of Primordial Black Holes: An RVB Residue Formulation of Thermal Formation and Nonequilibrium Evolution
papers.abstract: We establish a controlled, local, and quasi-stationary thermodynamic framework for neutral, nonrotating primordial black holes (PBHs) by combining a local residue prescription with the thermodynamicization of gravitational dynamics. For a nonextremal spherical horizon, we demonstrate that the positive residue of a meromorphic one-form directly determines the inverse Hawking temperature. Applying the first law of thermodynamics recovers the standard Schwarzschild temperature and Bekenstein-Hawking entropy under standard normalization. The resulting entropy defines an off-shell canonical exponent, which reveals that equilibrium thermal production of PBHs is exponentially suppressed in a radiation-dominated universe, thereby confirming that the standard density-perturbation collapse criterion remains the primary formation mechanism. For post-formation evolution, we adopt a detailed-balance mass law, prove the validity of the generalized second law of thermodynamics, and express the evolution dynamics as a free-energy gradient flow where the moving mass acts as an instantaneous evaporation-accretion threshold. Finally, we derive explicit first-order shifts for the temperature, entropy, thermal saddle, and nucleation exponent under small analytic deformations of the residue.

papers.title: Ordering Multivariate Time Series by Volatility Memory: A Temporal Convolutional Approach to Volatility Heredity
papers.abstract: Volatility dynamics can carry information about temporal relationships that is not apparent in the conditional mean. Extracting this information is difficult because the persistence of each variable can obscure its dependence on other variables. This paper presents QS-TCN, a method for ordering multivariate time series that combines statistical estimates of volatility memory with temporal convolutional learning. Persistence estimates obtained by quasi-maximum likelihood and temporal modes extracted by the Matrix Pencil method define structured filters within the network. Together with learned filters, they represent the history of the target and support comparisons of directional evidence between variables. These comparisons are combined into a global order of precedence, which does not identify a causal graph. The method is evaluated on synthetic systems with linear and nonlinear volatility interactions and on the Finance and fMRI benchmarks, whose reference relations are known. Across the four synthetic volatility regimes studied, QS-TCN reaches a higher mean ordering quality than an external lead--lag ordering and its squared-input adaptation, although the gain over the adaptation is uncertain in two regimes. Applications to currency, gold and cryptocurrency markets are reported descriptively.

papers.title: First Overlap Formulation and Perturbative Results for Supersymmetric QCD
papers.abstract: We present a lattice formulation of N=1 supersymmetric QCD (SQCD) based on overlap fermions, providing a discretization consistent with the Ginsparg-Wilson relation. Particular emphasis is placed on the construction of Yukawa terms that preserve a lattice-modified chiral symmetry involving overlap quarks and gluinos. To realize this modified chiral symmetry in the Yukawa sector, we follow Lüscher's strategy and introduce auxiliary Dirac and Majorana fermionic fields for the quark and gluino fields, respectively. After functional integration over these auxiliary fields, ultralocal interaction terms arise as additional contributions to the lattice action. Within this framework, and using the Wilson gauge action for gluons, we also carry out one-loop perturbative calculations. In particular, we compute the self-energies of the quark, gluon, gluino, and squark fields in the presence of quark and squark masses, enabling an unambiguous determination of the corresponding field and mass counterterms on the lattice. This work provides a robust foundation for future perturbative determinations of the fine-tunings of the gauge, Yukawa, and quartic couplings, and already shows, as expected, a reduction in the number of required counterterms relative to Wilson-type fermions.

papers.title: Designing Public Information for Strategic Advice
papers.abstract: A principal chooses an action using advice from an expert who privately knows local conditions. Before receiving advice, she can commission a public study of an independent state, such as future demand, that changes the expected conflict between their preferred actions. We show that the communication protocol determines the optimal study. Under optimal mediation, the value of advice is convex in conflict, making full revelation optimal. Under commitment to an action rule, the principal may prefer no information, while informative optimal studies include a report certifying high conflict. Under unmediated cheap talk, changes in the number of equilibrium messages create upward kinks in the value of advice. Optimal studies avoid interior communication thresholds and can induce two distant communication regimes while skipping every regime in between, strictly outperforming both full revelation and no information. When the principal retains the raw data, selective public disclosure can improve advice without sacrificing forecasting precision. We discuss implications for fiscal forecasts and spending agencies.

papers.title: Nonlinear optimal stopping and domineering claims
papers.abstract: We study nonlinear optimal stopping and domineering claims in a Brownian--Poisson filtration, under a nonlinear evaluation induced by a Lipschitz BSDE driver satisfying a comparison condition. A nonlinear domineering claim is a strong $\mathcal{E}^f$-martingale dominating the reward process at every stopping time. We first establish the existence of such claims for every optional reward in $\mathcal{S}^2$. For left-limited, right-upper semicontinuous rewards, we prove a local dual representation at every stopping time: the nonlinear optimal stopping value equals the essential infimum of the values of all domineering claims defined on the remaining stochastic interval. This infimum is attained by a claim constructed from the associated reflected BSDE. We further show that a global domineering claim attains the value at a prescribed stopping time if and only if the reflection processes have accumulated no increase up to that time, with the appropriate endpoint convention. When the reward is right-upper semicontinuous in $\mathcal{E}^f$-expectation and the family of contact times is nonempty, its essential infimum is optimal. Under strict comparison, we also establish a necessary contact condition for optimality. No convexity assumption on the driver is required.

papers.title: Laser fabrication of vibrating microcavities on silicon: Formation dynamics and frequency tunability
papers.abstract: Laser processing of silicon has long since become a standard method for wafer dicing, surface texturing, re-crystallization after ion implantation, as well as surface amorphization, to name a few examples. Here, we introduce a novel concept, the fabrication of vibrating microcavities in a commercial platform, Si wafers covered by a thick SiO2 layer, acting as a membrane. We demonstrate that by exposing our material system to single ultrashort laser pulses above the evaporation threshold of Si, a controlled delamination of the cover layer without fracture can be achieved, leading to the formation of a microcavity accompanied by a surface bulging up to 1.5 micrometer. The formation dynamics of the microcavities has been investigated by time-resolved optical probe techniques. Ultrafast pump-probe microscopy resolves the initial stages of substrate melting, the onset of layer expansion followed by relaxation. Real-time reflectivity measurements with nanosecond resolution resolve the long lived, highly complex oscillation process of the membrane, extending over tens of microseconds. The formed cavities can be re-excited at low fluence without damage or degradation, featuring vibrations at single frequencies with high Q factors. The frequencies can be tuned continuously from 8 MHz up to 19 MHz by adjusting the fabrication fluence. A simple classical model is found to well describe the behavior of the membranes. Our results pave the way for applications in micro- and nanooptics and acoustics, in great part due to the commercial availability of the Si-SiO2 platform and the simplicity of the fabrication method. An extension to the field of microelectromechanical system (MEMS) of this technology is proposed.

papers.title: Comparing Classification and Feature Learning by Analyzing Their Loss Functions in Normalized Spaces with Different Scale Factors
papers.abstract: Classification and feature learning are two closely interrelated fundamental tasks. Feature learning in supervised settings is typically achieved by training classification models, under the common assumption that higher classification accuracy implies better feature quality. In this paper, we first point out that classification accuracy reflects the sample-wise local properties of a model on a dataset, whereas feature learning aims to learn features with good dataset-level global properties, such as intra-class compactness and inter-class separability. From the first principle of feature learning, we redesign the binary cross-entropy (BCE) loss, a counterpart of the cross-entropy (CE) loss used in classification. Then, in normalized feature space, we analyze the minima of the BCE and CE losses and show that both can lead to neural collapse, where sample features from different classes become maximally compact and maximally separated. More importantly, by investigating the convergence behaviors of the two losses as the scale factor $γ$ varies in the normalized space, we reveal how classification accuracy and feature quality change differently across spaces of different sizes. Under a fixed training strategy, a very large $γ$ achieves perfect classification accuracy but slows convergence toward the ideal feature geometry, whereas a very small $γ$ makes classification highly sensitive to small perturbations. A moderate $γ$ is therefore necessary for simultaneously achieving reliable classification and well-structured features. Extensive experiments validate these findings and demonstrate that BCE loss exhibits advantages in long-tail and open-set recognitions, as it better aligns with the global requirements of feature learning.

papers.title: Global well-posedness for the energy-critical focusing NLS on $\mathbb T^3$
papers.abstract: We prove global well-posedness for the focusing quintic nonlinear Schrödinger equation on the standard three-dimensional torus for initial data below the mass-corrected energy and Sobolev-norm thresholds determined by the Euclidean ground state. This gives a subthreshold focusing counterpart to the defocusing theorem of Ionescu and Pausader. The proof combines the periodic profile analysis with the recent nonradial Euclidean scattering theorem of Su and Zhao. The mass correction yields an invariant region and a nonnegative energy decomposition, placing every Euclidean profile below both ground-state thresholds. Uniform bounds on finite intervals follow from a contradiction argument on shrinking time intervals.

papers.title: Fix One, Miss Another: Leveraging Historical Bug Fixes to Uncover Residual Bugs in Database Systems
papers.abstract: Database management systems (DBMSs) implement SQL constructs through grammar-driven dispatch handlers. Although handlers for syntactic siblings implement different SQL constructs, they often share a common implementation pattern, including argument extraction, type checking, and permission validation. Consequently, a bug fix that hardens the handler exercised by a historical bug may leave the corresponding logic in sibling handlers vulnerable to the same semantic flaw. We refer to such defects as sibling bugs. Despite the structural similarity among sibling handlers, existing bug-finding techniques rarely exploit historical fixes to systematically uncover these related defects. We present Reaper, a novel approach for detecting sibling bugs guided by historical bug fixes. Reaper first analyzes a bug fix to infer a trigger profile, which characterizes the conditions under which the defect is exposed, and a validation profile, which captures the semantic evidence needed to distinguish buggy behavior from correct behavior. It then projects the trigger profile onto syntactic siblings through grammar-guided test mutation, generating tests that exercise corresponding semantic paths in sibling handlers. Finally, Reaper validates suspicious behaviors using the inferred validation profile through a staged validation process, reducing false positives caused by complex DBMS behavior. We evaluate Reaper on four widely used DBMSs, including MariaDB, MySQL, OceanBase, and CockroachDB. Reaper uncovers 61 previously unknown bugs, of which 57 have been confirmed by developers and 13 have been fixed at the time of writing. These results demonstrate that historical bug fixes contain actionable semantic knowledge that can be systematically transferred across syntactic siblings to uncover otherwise overlooked defects.

papers.title: A continuum model of a diffusive compressible gas - Kinetic theory and real gases
papers.abstract: Using kinetic theory of gases, we derive the diffusive compressible Euler (dcE) model for ideal gases. The derivation covers all steps from the particle description of a gas, to macroscopic averages, to a discrete system of conservative balance equations in finite volumes, to the system of partial dif- ferential equations. Along the way, we discuss the modelling assumptions, and derive approximations of the diffusion coefficient. In the next part, we discuss the modifications needed to model real gases. In particular, we propose a tentative model for intermolecular friction forces.

papers.title: FALCON (FERMI-ALMA Calibrator ObservatioN): Cross-matching ALMA Calibrators with Fermi-LAT Blazars
papers.abstract: Blazars are active galactic nuclei with relativistic jets closely aligned with our line of sight, producing Doppler-boosted emission from radio to gamma rays. Millimeter emission near the synchrotron self-absorption turnover probes compact regions at the jet base, yet large statistical studies in this regime remain limited. We construct the FALCON (FERMI--ALMA Calibrator ObservatioN) catalogue, a millimeter-selected blazar sample by cross-matching the ALMA Calibrator Source Catalogue with the Third Data Release of the Fourth LAT AGN Catalog (4LAC-DR3). After removing duplicates, we obtain 949 unique gamma-ray-associated sources, corresponding to approximately 25 % of the 4LAC-DR3 blazar population. For the subset with available redshift measurements, we compute millimeter and gamma-ray luminosities and find a strong, statistically significant correlation that remains robust after accounting for redshift effects. Fermi-detected blazars exhibit systematically flatter millimeter spectral indices than gamma-ray non-detected ALMA calibrators, while the redshift-controlled luminosity correlation becomes progressively weaker from high-synchrotron-peaked BL Lacs toward flat-spectrum radio quasars. These results indicate an intrinsic connection between millimeter and gamma-ray emission, consistent with a common origin in relativistic jets governed by Doppler boosting and time-averaged jet power.

papers.title: Extending Reasoning in Typed Decision Models via Looping
papers.abstract: Typed decision models choose among a fixed set of answer options in a single forward pass, so unlike generative language models they cannot spend more test-time compute on hard inputs by generating more tokens. Looping a block of layers offers this compute in latent space without adding parameters, but prior work found no gain from loops retrofitted into conventionally pretrained models. We show that such loops help when trained together with the decision model. Our method, RELOAD (retrofitted loops for adaptive decisions), fine-tunes a pretrained encoder or decoder with a damped loop over its middle block and a lightweight controller picks the number of passes adaptively for each input. Across six models from 0.4B to 4B parameters, looping improves both accuracy and calibration, mostly on problems that need longer chains of reasoning than any seen in training, where encoders gain up to 23 points. Neither matched training compute nor more data closes this gap, and separate layers for each pass come close only with nearly twice the parameters. The controller keeps most of the gain at about three quarters of the compute.

papers.title: Evaluating Token Probabilities as Confidence Estimators in Human Behavior Simulations: A Case Study in Luxembourgish Next Like Prediction
papers.abstract: As large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to simulate human behavior, their operational validity is typically assessed through accuracy alone, implicitly treating human behavior as deterministic. We argue that on noisy digital trace data, a model's performance depends not only on predicting the correct outcome but on its calibration. We present a case study testing whether the token probabilities of open-weight LLMs can serve as confidence estimates in a Next Like Prediction task: predicting how a user of the Luxembourgish news platform RTL.lu rates a comment, conditioned on their prior interactions. Evaluating Ministral 3 (3B, 8B), we find that, with in-context learning only, the tested models are overconfident and are outperformed on accuracy and calibration by a simple statistical baseline. Accuracy and calibration do not move together: scaling from 3B to 8B improves accuracy while degrading calibration, and longer behavioral histories raise accuracy while confidence declines. Task-specific supervised fine-tuning acts as an effective calibration intervention, reducing Expected Calibration Error from 0.2 to 0.006 while improving accuracy from 0.536 to 0.758. We conclude that confidence estimation should be evaluated alongside accuracy to improve validity when using LLM-based agents.

papers.title: Data-driven current control of modular multilevel converter-based HVDC transmission system
papers.abstract: Model-based design (MBD) is a mature framework for designing the current controllers of modular multilevel converters (MMCs) in high-voltage direct current (HVDC) transmission systems. In MBD, linear state-space models are preferred for their good trade-off between accurate dynamics prediction and simplicity. However, first-principle derivations often neglect relevant MMC dynamics, which can hinder controller performance. Data-driven (DD) methods can deliver less biased models that capture parameter uncertainties, control-loop interactions, and grid dynamics, yet they remain under-exploited for controlling MMC currents. This paper studies DD current control method based on integral Subspace Predictive Control (iSPC), synthesized directly from input--output data measured in a high fidelity real-time digital simulator (RTDS), and proposes an initial guideline outlining the main steps for its systematic application to MMC current control. The proposed iSPC is compared against state-of-the-art DD solution, and the findings are validated through simulation studies in MATLAB/Simulink.

papers.title: On the classification of $2$-distance-primitive graphs of small valency
papers.abstract: A non-complete vertex-transitive graph is called 2-distance-primitive if a vertex stabilizer acts primitively on both the first and second distance neighborhoods of the vertex. Recently, Ruan, Liu and Jin [Discrete Math. 347 (2024), 113978] showed that every connected 2-distance-primitive graph of valency at most 9 either belongs to certain known families or satisfies a collection of further restrictions, with the socle of a vertex stabilizer isomorphic to $\mathrm{PSL}(2,7)$ or $\mathrm{PSL}(2,8)$. In this paper, we resolve these remaining cases and thereby obtain a complete classification of connected 2-distance-primitive graphs of valency at most 9. We also give a short proof of the main result of Ruan, Liu and Jin and identify additional graphs omitted from their list.

papers.title: Over-the-Scene Computation: Illumination-Programmed Functional Sensing of Unresolvable Populations
papers.abstract: Decisions about dense populations depend on how much will cross a boundary by a deadline and when the first member arrives. Conventional radar forms a range-Doppler map, whose cells add noise and whose detections merge unresolved members. We introduce over-the-scene computation, where illumination makes the scene compute such functionals without resolving members. With random echo phases, a correlator's mean output energy sums member reflectivities weighted by a kernel set by the waveform and template. The waveform's ambiguity function is this computation's transfer function, determining computable functionals and their noise cost. One readout aggregates members over a small delay-Doppler area but along a line segment growing with duration, longest for the chirp of matching slope among constant-envelope waveforms. Members predicted to share a range lie on such a line, so a chirp's mean beat spectrum is the predicted range profile at a look-ahead horizon set by its rate. For unbiased estimation, a Cramer-Rao bound over all equal-energy waveforms favors resolving members above unit signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) and grouping weaker ones into unit-SNR sets. At 0.65 members per cell, -10 dB member SNR, and one sweep, the chirp's bin sum inside the boundary comes within 16% of this bound in root-mean-square error and, with 77 times fewer samples per horizon, outperforms every unbiased estimator from a coherent processing interval of equal dwell, bandwidth, and energy. No finite set of waveform-template probes determines an unconstrained Rayleigh-fluctuating population's first arrival, but bisection localizes it if first arrivals outweigh later arrivals' sidelobes.

papers.title: O$^2$PD: Overlap-Gated On-Policy Distillation on Reliable Prefix
papers.abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) supplies dense token-level supervision by aligning a student to the teacher's next-token distribution on its own generated rollouts. Existing works mostly implement top-$k$ OPD, applying reverse Kullback-Leibler ($\RKL$) divergence between the teacher's and the student's renormalized distributions over teacher top-$k$ support. However, the teacher scores student-generated rollouts that are inherently off-policy for itself, leaving the reliability of its next-token guidance unclear. Restricting the divergence to the teacher top-$k$ support also discards the remaining mass outside that support. These gaps leave two questions implicit: 1) which tokens to align, and 2) how to align those tokens. To answer these questions, we propose Overlap-gated On-Policy Distillation (O$^{2}$PD). As for 1), we quantitatively analyze the reliability of teacher supervision and find that alignment on the student's trajectory prefix is more reliable than alignment on the full context. Therefore, our O$^{2}$PD is applied only to the 20\% prefix tokens of each student rollout. As for 2), we theoretically characterize two problems of top-$k$ OPD: the \emph{Teacher-support Uncovering} and the \emph{Dominant-Mode Mismatch}. Based on these analyses, we propose two support strategies: the \emph{Reset Support} strategy attaches a reset atom to every token, pooling mass outside the teacher top-$k$, and the \emph{Support Convergence} strategy converges the support to the already aligned intersection. Our O$^{2}$PD employs the designed overlap-gated $α$-divergence to interpolate between mode-covering and mode-seeking for per-token alignment, where the overlap is used as a gate to switch the support and adaptively modulate $α$.

papers.title: Seeing Beyond the Next Step: World-Model-Guided Human-Like Navigation in Multi-Agent Scenes
papers.abstract: Selecting a next motion in a populated scene is not just a matter of avoiding what is currently in the way: an action can be locally feasible yet drift onto the road instead of the crosswalk, cut into a stream of crossing pedestrians, or bottleneck a narrow passage. These failure modes are invisible from the current state alone, and acting on them requires reasoning about what each candidate action will cause. World models offer exactly this, namely action-conditioned predictions of the future, but rolling them out at every decision step is a cost deployable navigation systems cannot pay, and the field has largely traded foresight for speed. We argue this is a false dichotomy. The natural place for a world model in human-aware navigation is at training time, as a preference oracle that distills foresight into a fast policy, rather than at inference time, as an online planner. We pair a discrete visual action prior with two task-aligned world models, one for nearby social dynamics and one for future scene semantics, that score candidate actions by their predicted consequences and refine the policy through group-relative preference distillation. At deployment, both world models are removed and the policy acts in a single forward pass. Across five held-out evaluation scenarios, this yields navigation that is simultaneously safer, more socially and group-coherent, and more goal-directed than strong reactive and learned baselines, with naive observers rating the resulting motion as more human-like. Taken together, our findings point to a different approach for bringing world-model foresight into deployable agents: not accelerating rollouts, but amortizing them into the policy so that the cost of looking ahead is confined to training. Project page: https://seoneun.github.io/-NeurIPS-2026-Seeing-Beyond-the-Next-Step/

papers.title: Unified design of short mode-evolution couplers
papers.abstract: Short mode-evolution couplers have been designed with several seemingly different approaches, including fast quasi-adiabatic dynamics (FAQUAD), counter-diabatic (CD) driving realized by tailoring waveguide widths and spacing, CD driving realized by axis bending, and numerical optimization of the coupler geometry. Using exact two-mode coupled-mode theory in the Kramers--Henneberger frame of the bent coupler, we show that these approaches belong to the same design space. The three geometric parameters, width difference, spacing, and axis tilt, act on the light through two functions only: the coupling strength, set by the spacing, and an effective detuning, set by the width difference and the axis curvature. The gauge, bent, and mixed realizations of a CD coupler are therefore the same device and have the same bandwidth. The bandwidth is set by the angle $χ$ between the light and the field that steers it on the Bloch sphere, integrated along the device as $\int\sin^2χdz$, and for a CD coupler this integral is set by the reference alone. This leads to a lithography-aware design rule: make the reference as adiabatic as the minimum gap allows, by narrowing its spacing at the anticrossing, and let exact CD suppress the remaining nonadiabatic coupling. In beam propagation method (BPM) simulations on a polymer platform, a 500\um{} coupler designed this way, without numerical optimization, maintains ${>}99\%$ transfer over 274~nm at a minimum edge gap of 1.05\um, compared with 150~nm for the CD coupler of a fixed-spacing reference at nearly the same gap. Particle swarm optimization of the geometry with BPM in the loop does not exceed the design rule. Three-dimensional BPM of the BCB channel waveguides also confirms these conclusions.

papers.title: Singular values of iterated Aluthge transforms of compact operators
papers.abstract: Yamazaki proved that the norms of the iterated Aluthge transforms of an operator converge to its spectral radius, and Ando showed that for matrices the singular values of the iterates converge to the moduli of the eigenvalues. We prove that the latter holds for every compact operator on a Hilbert space and every generalized Aluthge transform $Δ_t$ with $0<t<1$: for every $j$, the $j$-th singular value of the $n$-th iterate converges to $|λ_j(T)|$, and the products of the $k$ largest singular values, as well as the Ky Fan norms, decrease monotonically to their limits. This is the Aluthge counterpart of the Yamamoto--Davis theorem. We also determine the limit in the Schatten $p$-norm whenever $T$ belongs to a strictly smaller Schatten class.

papers.title: Separability and lower bounds of concurrence via symmetric measurement correlations
papers.abstract: The detection and quantification of quantum entanglement is a central issue in quantum information science, particularly for unknown quantum states. Based on symmetric measurement correlation matrices, we present a family of separability criteria that can be experimentally applied without state tomography, and recover some related existing criteria as special cases. Using the constructed correlation matrices, we further derive a class of lower bounds of concurrence. Through illustrative examples, we demonstrate that our criteria outperform some existing separability criteria in entanglement detection, and that the obtained lower bounds on concurrence are tighter than known counterparts.

papers.title: Dual-Arm Tabletop Rearrangement with Movable Stacking and Gap-Aware Push Transfers
papers.abstract: Object rearrangement in cluttered tabletop scenes is challenging, especially in wide workspaces where dual-arm systems improve coverage and efficiency. Limited free space often necessitates buffering, while objects near or across the shared reachability region of the manipulators must be transferred under careful coordination to avoid inter-arm collisions. Conventional inter-arm transfer typically relies on a fixed handoff configuration, which constrains where and how objects are exchanged, enforces spatiotemporal synchronization of the arms, and reduces flexibility in dense layouts. This paper presents a dual-arm rearrangement framework that combines movable stacking with Gap-Aware Push Transfer for asynchronous cross-boundary exchange. The method scans the shared boundary to identify collision-free transfer gaps, places an object near a selected crossing point, and then pushes it into the receiving workspace without requiring simultaneous interaction between the two arms. A joint Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS)-based planner coordinates both manipulators while reasoning over buffering and transfer decisions, and execution cost is used after planning to assess the resulting plan. Experiments show that the proposed method shortens joint execution sequences and becomes increasingly advantageous over a fixed handoff baseline as scene density increases, achieving lower execution cost in denser scenes while remaining competitive in lighter ones.

papers.title: Global existence of solutions to the 2D compressible nematic liquid crystal flows with large initial data and vacuum
papers.abstract: For periodic initial data that allow vacuum, we establish the global-in-time existence of solutions to the 2D compressible nematic liquid crystal flows, under the condition that the bulk viscosity coefficient is sufficiently large and a geometric angular constraint is imposed on the initial direction field. Our results remain valid for arbitrarily large initial energy. Furthermore, under appropriate additional assumptions imposed on the pressure, we also establish the uniqueness of the constructed solutions.

papers.title: Uplink Enhancement for Low-Altitude UAVs via Active RISs Under Existing Cellular Infrastructure
papers.abstract: The proliferation of low-altitude aerial Internet of Things applications, such as UAV-based sensing/monitoring, demands high-performance uplinks, yet terrestrial-optimized cellular networks with downtilted base station (BS) antennas form coverage holes that severely degrade aerial uplink. To address this challenge without modifying infrastructure, active reconfigurable intelligent surfaces (RISs) are introduced. Unlike existing studies with complicated active RIS optimizations, we conduct a detailed noise analysis to simplify the transmission design. By deploying one active RIS per BS sector to fully exploit multi-sector reception, we develop a joint sector maximal signal combining scheme that improves signal quality through diversity gain. Active RISs introduce amplifier noise, raising questions about their net benefit. We derive an upper bound on the power ratio between RIS-introduced noise and BS-inherent noise, revealing that the impact of RIS noise is negligible under typical operating conditions. Based on this insight, we maximize a derived lower bound of the received signal-to-noise ratio by sequentially designing the amplitude and phase of reflection coefficients with closed-form expressions. Simulation results validate the theoretical analysis on negligible RIS-introduced noise in typical systems and demonstrate that under the same array gain, a larger RIS size rather than a higher reflection gain is preferred for enhancing the low-altitude uplink transmission.

papers.title: Static Recovery Is Not Dynamic Stability: Dynamics-Aware Benchmarking of Protein Motif Scaffolding
papers.abstract: Protein motif scaffolding benchmarks assess whether generative models can build scaffolds around functionally important residues. Their conclusions depend on which motifs are tested and which criteria define success. Existing benchmarks typically use small hand-curated motif sets and static refolding criteria, but protein function often depends on conformational ensembles and transitions. Here, we address both benchmark scope and success criteria. We introduce BILBY-PRO, a systematically derived benchmark of structurally conserved functional motifs from PROSITE-linked experimental structures, comprising 220 cases from 174 PROSITE motif-pattern entries. Evaluating six recent scaffold-generation models reveals distinct patterns in target coverage and unique-solution yield: RFDiffusion and Proteina solve more targets, whereas ESM3 produces more unique successful scaffolds on the targets it solves. We further introduce BILBY-MD, a reference-based all-atom molecular dynamics evaluation framework. Applied to statically solved designs from the original MotifBench benchmark, it compares motif drift, scaffold drift, motif-contact preservation, and motif-dihedral free-energy landscapes against reference simulations. Of 55 statically solved model-problem pairs, 31 satisfy our MD-supported criterion and only 8 pass all checks. Compact, self-contained motifs are often MD-supported, whereas interface-like or context-dependent motifs fail more frequently. Static refolding success therefore provides useful evidence of local motif recovery but does not establish dynamical fidelity of the full scaffold. BILBY highlights three complementary axes of motif-scaffolding evaluation: target coverage, unique-solution yield, and MD-supported dynamical fidelity.

papers.title: Continued Training of Continuous Language Flows with Token Identity Squared Supervision
papers.abstract: Diffusion and flow models have recently been extended to language modeling, generating text through continuous denoising in token embedding spaces. Pretrained models provide token representations and contextual prediction capabilities, but improving generation with limited additional training requires an appropriate connection between supervision and continuous generation. Continuous MSE evaluates a predicted vector obtained by weighting token embeddings with predicted probabilities; different probability distributions can yield the same vector and are therefore indistinguishable under this objective. We propose Token Identity Brier Flow (TIBF), which applies squared supervision directly to token identities when continuing pretrained language flows. TIBF combines network scores with token-matching scores under a Gaussian observation model, supervises token probabilities using the Brier loss, and uses probability-weighted embeddings for continuous generation. With fixed token embeddings, we show that the squared error between predicted token probabilities and the true posterior bounds the squared errors of continuous denoising predictions and flow velocities. A risk decomposition separates uncertainty inherent in the observation from posterior fitting error, motivating continued training that preserves pretrained embeddings and focuses on probability prediction. We also establish convergence to token embeddings under ideal predictions and sufficient conditions for local convergence with prediction error. From common pretrained initializations and under matched continuation budgets, frozen-embedding TIBF achieves Gen.PPL values of 33.96 on OWT and 81.17 on LM1B, outperforming continuous-MSE and CE continuation controls. It attains the lowest Gen.PPL at every tested sampling budget on both datasets, together with the lowest repetition rate on LM1B.

papers.title: Evaluating Language Model Features for Zero-Shot Time-Series Anomaly Detection Under Isolation Assumption
papers.abstract: Time-Series Anomaly Detection (TSAD) is a fundamentally challenging task: it is unsupervised, requires high local precision capabilities, and suffers from limited labelled data. Recent work has explored adapting Large Language Models (LLMs) to time-series via cross-modal transfer. However, existing approaches are poorly suited to Multivariate TSAD (MTSAD), as tokenisation often obscures fine-grained temporal and variables structures, and most methods optimise auxiliary objectives such as forecasting or reconstruction. We posit that these surrogate objectives become unreliable as model capacity increases. Highly expressive models risk reconstructing or forecasting anomalies, undermining the foundations of both strategies. Instead, we propose to use LLMs purely as feature extractors and directly analyse their induced feature spaces. In this work, investigate the ability of LLMs to provide useful representations for MTSADs in a zero-shot setting through classification. To this end, we study the separability of the extracted features, under the assumption that anomalous features should be isolated from normal ones. We analyse their temporal and contextual discriminative ability using simple step-wise tokenisation schemes, with one time-step per token, which preserve fine-grained local information. Their usability for MTSAD is assessed using an unsupervised Isolation Forest, enabling a direct evaluation of the resulting representation quality. We further investigate whether the observed performance can be attributed to the language-related pre-training of the LLMs or arises independently of it. Our results provide empirical insight into the ability of LLMs to represent multivariate time-series for anomaly detection and highlight broader applications of cross-modal foundation models.

papers.title: Graph Symbolic Distillation: Decoding Graph Data into Interpretable Formulas across Materials and Chemistry
papers.abstract: Graph data provide a natural representation of the interconnected structures and interactions underlying many chemical and materials systems. Graph neural networks (GNNs) can learn complex relationships from such data, yet translating these representations into interpretable descriptors and scientific insights remains challenging. Here we introduce graph symbolic distillation (GSD), a framework for decoding graph data into interpretable symbolic formulas. GSD identifies task-relevant message-passing architectures and distills their learned transformations while preserving graph connectivity and aggregation operations. Across three case studies spanning bulk materials, molecules, and surfaces, GSD not only recovers expert-defined descriptors from elementary node and edge features, but also reveals relationships emerging from their organization in complex graphs: extremal local geometric descriptors for band gap variations in $γ$-CsPbI$_3$, a local polarity--size relationship underlying hydration free energy, and site-specific electronic--connectivity coupling in multidentate adsorption. GSD thus provides a general route from graph data to interpretable descriptors and new, testable scientific insights.

papers.title: Multimodal Information Interactions Bottleneck for Multimodal Self-Supervised Learning
papers.abstract: Multimodal self-supervised learning is challenged by heterogeneity, unequal informativeness, and complex information interactions across multimodal data sources such as images, text, audio, and tabular data. While contrastive methods effectively align shared semantics, they typically rely on strong multi-view redundancy assumptions, overlooking modality-specific and synergistic information, thus leading to suboptimal representations. We propose the Multimodal Information Interactions Bottleneck (MIIB), a principled framework grounded in Partial Information Decomposition that explicitly encodes redundant, unique, and synergistic information within multimodal interactions. MIIB employs a dual-path model architecture for modality-specific encoding and multimodal fusion, optimized using surrogate tractable entropy-based objectives that enforce minimal sufficient representations without requiring explicit mutual information estimation. By leveraging variational bounds and score-based entropy estimation, MIIB efficiently captures complex cross-modal interactions while suppressing superfluous information. Experiments across diverse benchmarks demonstrate consistent improvements over state-of-the-art multimodal self-supervised methods. Code is available at https://github.com/wanglingzaishi/MIIB.

papers.title: Pediatric ECG foundation model via adult-to-pediatric fine-tuning: downstream tasks and clinical evaluation
papers.abstract: Pediatric electrocardiogram (ECG) interpretation is complicated by age-dependent electrophysiological changes that limit direct transfer of adult AI models. We asked whether an adult ECG foundation model could be adapted to pediatric ECGs. Using 339,563 12-lead ECGs from 238,189 children, we compared direct application, pediatric fine-tuning, and training from scratch under an identical architecture. Direct transfer was poor (mean AUC 0.8256). Fine-tuning reached 0.9695, above de novo training (0.9661), and attained 0.9079 using only 1% of training data. On 10,999 external ECGs, fine-tuning achieved a mean AUC of 0.9385 across 30 labels. It generalized to age regression (MAE 1.12 years) and congenital heart disease classification (AUC 0.9562). Across 17 clinicians and 100 cases, diagnostic accuracy rose from 56.8% to 65.4% (p < 0.001) and did not decline when AI erred. Adult ECG foundation models require pediatric adaptation; fine-tuning offers a data-efficient route to scalable pediatric ECG AI.

papers.title: Copula-Based Dependence Modeling for Resilient 6G Multi-Hop Wireless Networks
papers.abstract: Reliable operation of multi-hop wireless networks requires accounting for statistical dependence among link failures caused by common propagation conditions and shared network components. This paper develops a copula-based framework for modeling node-induced dependence among link-level signal-to-noise ratios and quantifying its effect on end-to-end outage. By separating marginal fading distributions from the dependence structure, the framework captures nonlinear and tail-dependent coupling beyond conventional correlation-based models. Exact outage expressions are derived for primary-backup configurations involving edge-disjoint paths and paths with shared links. We then characterize the conditional outage probability of each candidate backup path given a primary-path failure, jointly accounting for node-induced dependence and shared-link failures. In high-reliability regimes, we derive a first-order score that decomposes conditional outage into terms associated with marginal path outage, shared links, and node-induced dependence, enabling efficient dependence-aware backup-path selection. We also establish sufficient conditions under which the first-order and exact selection rules identify the same backup path. Numerical results validate the analysis and show that copula families with the same Kendall's $τ$ can yield markedly different outage behavior because of their different tail-dependence properties. In particular, lower-tail dependence and path overlap can substantially reduce redundancy gains and reverse rankings based only on marginal outage probability.

papers.title: Anti-ribbon shaped Young diagram decomposition
papers.abstract: We introduce a sliding procedure on diagrams which splits the standard Young tableaux of a corner-crossed diagram, in particular of a skew shape, along a finite binary tree whose leaves are anti-ribbon diagrams. Combined with standardization, this yields a decomposition of semi-standard Young tableaux into tableaux of anti-ribbon shape, indexed by standard tableaux and governed by their descent sets. As applications, we obtain expansions of Schur functions and Schur multiple zeta functions in terms of their anti-ribbon type analogues; at the level of Schur functions, this is a tableau-level form of Gessel's fundamental quasisymmetric expansion.

papers.title: Solvable macroscopic models for populations of type I excitability neurons with Gaussian noise
papers.abstract: The dynamics of type I excitability neurons near the bifurcation point are governed by the model of quadratic integrate-and-fire neuron (QIF). The model of QIF subject to white Gaussian noise is abundant in statistical physics, since it not only reasonably reproduces the dynamics of some biological systems but also emerges in the problems of stochastic stability and in quantum mechanics of one-dimensional systems with quenched disorder. We derive the solution for the mean interspike interval of a QIF subject to additive Gaussian noise in terms of analytic functions, from the first passage time problem. On the basis of this solution, we construct analytical expressions for the firing rate and population-mean membrane potential in terms of the real and imaginary parts of a certain universal analytic function. With this function, we generalize theoretical results to heterogeneous populations with Lorentzian-distributed parameters. Implementation of theoretical results is demonstrated and examined for two problems: the interplay between chemical and electrical synapses, and the emergence of effective endogenous noise in sparse inhibitory networks. For the latter case, it is possible to cover the scenarios where the effective noise intensity depends on Lorentzian-distributed parameters, which is not feasible directly with the diffusion approximation.

papers.title: Selective Event Evidence and Persistent Temporal Priors for Event-Based Point Tracking
papers.abstract: Event cameras enable tracking under fast motion and challenging illumination. However, stable long-term point tracking remains challenging: event activity is sparse and varies with scene content and motion, complicating correspondence, while trajectory estimates can drift over long sequences. Together, these challenges motivate a tracker that selectively uses informative event evidence and retains trajectory constraints across temporal windows. We propose Selective Event Evidence and Persistent Temporal Priors (SEPT), an event-only framework for tracking any point (TAP) over long sequences. SEPT introduces two complementary modules: Task-Adaptive Event Evidence Modulation (TEEM) and Persistent Trajectory Prior (PTP). Using only tracking supervision, TEEM learns a bounded reliability field that weights the event tensor across space, time, and channels before feature extraction. PTP carries geometric information across overlapping windows by marginalizing a fixed local quadratic trajectory model with a Schur complement. Its visibility-aware correction refines overlap coordinates, while a clipped terminal velocity initializes coordinates at newly exposed timestamps. SEPT builds on the ETAP architecture. SEPT is trained exclusively on synthetic EventKubric data and evaluated on five datasets across TAP and feature tracking. Results show that SEPT outperforms the retrained ETAP baseline in average Jaccard for TAP and in feature age and expected feature age for feature tracking; it also surpasses several methods combining event and frame inputs on EC and EDS. The source code is publicly available at https://github.com/sssxxxkkkk/SEPT.

papers.title: AffectiveVLA: Safe and Intent-Aware VLA Control for Human-Humanoid Social Interaction
papers.abstract: Social touch interactions, such as handshakes, fist bumps, and hugs, require humanoid robots to infer human intent, generate contact-rich motions, and maintain safe physical contact. We present AffectiveVLA, an intent-gated Vision-Language-Action (VLA) pipeline deployed on a Unitree G1 humanoid with dexterous hands. A lightweight RGB-based model recognizes interaction intent from two onboard cameras and converts it into a language prompt for the VLA policy. Low-confidence predictions suppress motion execution, reducing unintended activations. During physical contact, interaction-specific compliance profiles adjust arm impedance, while an independent voice-triggered mechanism initiates a latched safe-stop procedure. Using VR teleoperation, we collected approximately 1,300 multimodal interaction episodes and fine-tuned four VLA models: GR00T, RLDX-1, Being-H0.5, and UnifoLM-VLA-0. On-robot evaluation identifies GR00T as the best-performing standalone model. Integrating intent recognition increases its macro-F1 score from 0.75 to 0.90, while the intent model achieves a p95 inference latency of 6.27 ms. These results demonstrate that explicit intent gating improves the reliability of VLA-based social interaction without compromising real-time operation.

papers.title: Fast and Accurate Hand Estimation in Pixels, Interaction and World Space
papers.abstract: Monocular hand mesh estimators commonly predict rig parameters and project the mesh to obtain 2D keypoints. We find that directly predicted 3D joints agree better with 2D predictions, and fitting a mesh to predicted points reduces mesh error. We present FAH (Fast and Accurate Hand Estimation), a family of models built on SAM 3D Body's hand branch through fine-tuning and feature distillation. The models predict corresponding 2D and 3D joints and surface points, fit MANO or MHR-Hand, and optionally estimate anatomical parts and contact without object geometry at inference. Causal refinement reduces acceleration error, and camera estimation places the hands in world space. Experiments show improvements in image-space alignment, hand geometry, contact estimation and world-space tracking over the evaluated baselines. The default ViT-L model runs at 65 fps with mesh fitting on an RTX 4070 Ti SUPER, or 49 fps with parts and contact enabled. The smallest ViT-S model reaches 125 fps without mesh fitting, parts or contact. Code: https://github.com/noahcao/FAH.

papers.title: Critical Curve for Three-Dimensional Radial Wave Systems with Distinct Speeds
papers.abstract: We study radially symmetric solutions to the three-dimensional semilinear wave system with distinct propagation speeds \[ u_{tt}-c_1^2Δu=|v_t|^p\ , \ v_{tt}-c_2^2Δv=|u_t|^q\ , \ c_1, c_2>0\ , c_1\neq c_2\ . \] For \(1<p,q<2\), we prove that \[ Γ(p,q) = 2+\max\left\{\frac1p,\frac1q\right\}-pq=0 \] is the exact critical curve separating small-data global existence from finite-time blow-up. More precisely, sufficiently small, compactly supported radial initial data give rise to global solutions when $Γ(p,q)<0$. On the other hand, for a class of initial data, the corresponding solutions blow up in finite time, with an upper bound for the lifespan, when $Γ(p,q)\geq 0$.

papers.title: AffineGS: Unlocking Accurate Geometry in 3DGS via Spatially Varying Affine Rectification
papers.abstract: 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) has become the leading approach for photorealistic novel view synthesis, yet its geometric accuracy lags behind its visual quality. Existing depth-guided methods attempt to resolve this by regularizing the optimization with monocular depth priors, typically using a single global scale-and-shift alignment. Crucially, we discover a fundamental flaw in this assumption: modern monocular depth networks systematically exhibit region-dependent, piecewise-linear distortions. This discovery invalidates standard global alignment strategies, which warp scene geometry by enforcing a single transform. To address this, we introduce a spatially varying affine rectification model that corrects monocular disparity into consistent metric depth using regionally smooth, edge-aware fields. We further derive a normal-aware regularizer that uses spatial gradients to couple the rectified disparity with 3DGS depth and normals. Across diverse experimental settings, our sensor-free method shows strong photometric quality of Gaussian Splatting while substantially improving geometric accuracy and outperforming state-of-the art geometry-focused methods.

papers.title: Signature of charge-3e tunneling in twisted cuprate Josephson junctions
papers.abstract: Cooper pairing is a fundamental aspect of superconductivity and results in charge transport with a basic unit of 2e (e is the electron charge). This basic unit can manifest itself as the denominator in the formula for Shapiro steps of ac Josephson effect-nhf/(2e), where h is the Planck constant, f is the ac frequency and n is an integer. Violation of this standard formula may suggest unconventional physics, such as nhf/4e for charge-4e superconductivity. Here, we report discovery of a new sequence of nhf/3e in twisted cuprate Josephson junctions. The microwave frequency/power, temperature, and current annealing dependences of this exotic sequence consistently point to hf/3e as the unit for Shapiro steps, indicating a Josephson tunneling process involving a trio of electrons (3e). This bunching of an odd number of charges distinguishes itself from well-established superconducting processes, which are carried by composite bosons made of an even number of charges. The unusual observations highlight the important interplay between competing charge orders in twisted bilayer systems.

papers.title: CAMP: Context-Aware Mapping and Placement for LLMs on 3D-IMC Arrays
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) incur severe memory-access overheads due to the cost of loading large weight matrices and key-value (KV) caches. Analog In-Memory Computing (AIMC) is an emerging solution that enables computation directly on static weights stored in memory, substantially reducing energy and latency. 3D-IMC further stacks memory arrays into vertical tiers, increasing capacity but revealing a new challenge: how weights are placed in memory determines which matrix-vector multiplications (MVMs) can execute concurrently, affecting latency and throughput. The concurrency aspect of 3D-IMC weight-mapping remains underexplored in the literature, leading to sub-optimal utilization of compute resources on 3D-IMC chips. In this context we propose CAMP (Context-Aware Mapping and Placement), an inference-context-aware weight mapping algorithm for 3D-IMC-based LLM accelerators. CAMP captures the potential resource contention resulting from the architecture, targeted network, and runtime context in a conflict matrix, enabling throughput-optimized weight mapping. This mapping is refined through a profiling-driven feedback loop that efficiently prunes the search space and returns optimized mappings within practical runtimes. CAMP is an offline, software-based solution requiring no hardware changes and improving 3D-IMC compute utilization from 42.4% to 60.3%, delivering up to 2.0x higher 3D-IMC throughput and 1.74x higher end-to-end throughput over state-of-the-art mapping algorithms.

papers.title: Towards Generalist Graph-Level Anomaly Detection
papers.abstract: Graph-level anomaly detection (GLAD) aims to identify graphs that deviate significantly from the majority. While recent advances have achieved competitive performance, existing approaches mainly follow a dataset-specific paradigm, requiring substantial in-domain data and training cost when applied to new application scenarios. This limits their scalability and practicality in real-world applications where labeled data is scarce and diverse domains are continuously emerging. In this paper, we investigate the problem of generalist GLAD, which seeks to learn a single unified model capable of detecting anomalous graphs across multiple domains with minimal supervision on the target data. This problem introduces key challenges, including learning transferable patterns from heterogeneous graph datasets and effective adaptation under limited supervision. To address these challenges, we propose GenGLAD, a generalist GLAD approach that leverages discriminative subgraph extraction as the core mechanism to learn transferable anomaly knowledge and enable efficient adaptation to new domains. Specifically, GenGLAD employs a graph neural network-based discriminative subgraph extraction model to learn the anomaly-discriminative substructures that distinguish anomalous and normal graphs across diverse domains. During the test-time adaptation phase, multi-dimensional discrepancies between the extracted subgraph and multi-level contextual information are calculated to characterize anomalies from multiple perspectives. For efficient adaptation, a lightweight scoring module is introduced to automatically decide the most informative signals, improving robustness against misleading patterns. Extensive experiments on diverse benchmark datasets demonstrate that the proposed approach achieves strong performance, superior generalization ability, and improved data efficiency compared to existing methods.

papers.title: FlyingDrones: A Dataset and Benchmark for Optical Flow Estimation from UAV motion
papers.abstract: Optical flow is an important cue for drone analysis in aerial surveillance, airspace monitoring, and long-range target tracking, where motion remains informative when appearance is weak. Estimating the motion of small Unmanned Aerial Vehicles, however, is difficult because distant targets occupy few pixels, have low contrast, and move against complex dynamic backgrounds. Standard optical-flow benchmarks emphasize large, object-centric motions and therefore do not characterize distant aerial targets well. We introduce FlyingDrones, a generated benchmark with dense ground-truth optical flow and segmentation masks derived from physically based rendering, and define resolution-normalized metrics (EPE Norm) that normalize flow by image dimensions. We evaluate 16 state-of-the-art model families on a motion- and size-stratified subset of 999 flow pairs at three resolutions. Every family recovers drone motion better than the zero-flow reference, but the gap between families widens with resolution: at 1920x1080, global-matching, recurrent, transformer, and short-window temporal models separate clearly from pyramid, classical, self-supervised, lightweight, and diffusion models. Within-family checkpoint spread is comparable to or larger than between-family spread, so the training curriculum is as important as the architecture. Two complementary studies test the benchmark beyond synthetic accuracy: a ground-truth-free motion-alignment evaluation on 21 cameras of real UAV footage shows that the synthetic ranking carries a moderate, significant signal about real-world performance (Spearman \r{ho} = 0.63 over 41 checkpoints) while the exact top ranks differ, and a fine-tuning study shows that 800 FlyingDrones pairs reduce held-out drone-region error by up to 37% and improve drone localization on the real footage for all four architectures tested.

papers.title: Towards Track Height Control in Additive Manufacturing on Porous Substrates: An Approach for System Identification and Controller Selection
papers.abstract: Additive manufacturing is transforming the creation of materials and parts, enabling the design and manufacturing of multifunctional parts with tailored properties. One compelling example is the combination of a porous core and a non-porous surface, which offers significant advantages in terms of weight reduction, material efficiency, strength and wear resistance. Directed Energy Deposition (DED) processes enable the transition from porous core to non-porous part surface by closing the pores. However, the surface-layer of porous substrates presents a substantial challenge to achieving consistent track heights during DED, directly impacting the final part geometry and performance. Therefore, precise control of the deposition process is crucial for realising the full potential of the multifunctional parts. In order to address this challenge, this work presents a conceptual approach for track height control during Laser-based Directed Energy Deposition (DED-LB) on porous substrates. First, the DED-LB process and the associated measurement setup are explained, along with a discussion of their limitations. The focus then shifts to the control problem, beginning with system identification to characterise the process dynamics. Subsequently, a selection of control strategies is investigated, as well as their compatibility with the process. This research provides a foundational step toward reliable additive manufacturing on porous substrates, and thus toward producing multifunctional parts.

papers.title: Distributed Optimization Involving Non-Lipschitzian, Linear Composite Functions: Unified Algorithm Design and Convergence Analysis
papers.abstract: This paper formulates a generic distributed nonsmooth optimization problem subject to edge-based equality constraints, local inequality constraints characterized by general convex functions, as well as globally coupling constraints including affine equality and nonlinear inequality. The terminal goal is to minimize the sum of local non-differentiable convex functions and proximable nonsmooth convex composite terms attached to linear operators, over networked multi-agent systems. This formulated framework not only applies in complex practical problems but also reduces to existing distributed optimization structures. To cope with technical issues caused by local linear mappings, potential multiple nonsmooth functions and coupling nonlinear constraints, we first derive a new local first-order condition, and further present a novel fully distributed optimization algorithm based on variable decompositions and proximal operators. Specifically, the proposed algorithm allows each agent to update states via local information exchange and through {locally fixed step-sizes}, and to find inexact solutions of subproblems without loss of convergence speed. In contrast to existing tailor-made algorithms for the bounded gradients of objective functions or affine constraints, our algorithm is capable of solving more practical cases involving general convex functions and nonlinear constraints. Under mild assumptions, the convergence rate $o(1/k)$ in terms of the optimality and successive-difference metrics is achieved, by constructing the equivalent variational inequalities of the proposed algorithm. Finally, numerical experiments on practical application problems illustrate the theoretical results.

papers.title: InfMasking: A Unified Variational Framework for Synergistic Multimodal Learning
papers.abstract: Multimodal models are expected to exploit synergistic information, that is, information available only when multiple modalities are observed together. In practice, however, a fusion module can fit the training objective by relying on a dominant modality or on information that modalities share, and the synergy between modalities is often left unused. We propose InfMasking, a unified multimodal learning framework based on Infinite Masking.
